subject: Mathematics
topic: Sampling distributions, uncertainty and confidence intervals
scope: Original introductory statistical inference. Assumptions are explicit; no claim is made that this covers a named university course or every examination specification.
prerequisites: Calculate and interpret a mean and standard deviation.
Distinguish a sample from a target population.
objectives: Distinguish a parameter, statistic and sampling distribution.
Explain standard error and the effect of sample size under stated assumptions.
Interpret a confidence procedure without turning it into a probability claim about a fixed parameter.

notes.heading: Parameters and repeated sampling
paragraphs: A population parameter is a numerical feature of the population or model of interest, such as a mean. A sample statistic is computed from the observed sample and is used to learn about that parameter. Different samples can produce different statistics even when they come from the same population. The sampling distribution describes this variation over repeated samples generated by a specified procedure. It is not the distribution of individual observations within one sample. Keep the target population, sampling procedure and statistic explicit before discussing an estimate's uncertainty.

notes.heading: Standard deviation and standard error
paragraphs: A standard deviation describes spread in a distribution. The standard error of a statistic is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution. For the mean of n independent observations with common finite population variance σ², the standard error is σ/√n. When σ is unknown, replacing it with the sample standard deviation gives an estimated standard error under appropriate conditions. The square-root relationship means that halving this standard error requires four times the sample size, not twice. Dependence, clustering, unequal sampling weights or a different statistic can require a different calculation. State the assumptions rather than treating the formula as universal.

notes.heading: Confidence procedures
paragraphs: A confidence interval is produced by a procedure designed to cover the fixed target parameter at a stated long-run rate under its assumptions. For a 95% procedure, approximately 95% of intervals constructed in repeated applications would contain the parameter if the procedure's conditions hold. After observing a particular interval, the fixed parameter is either inside it or outside it; the frequentist statement concerns the procedure's repeated-sampling performance. A Bayesian probability interval uses a different interpretation and requires additional modelling assumptions. Do not silently switch between these interpretations because both produce two endpoints.

notes.heading: Uncertainty is not the same as bias
paragraphs: A narrow interval does not guarantee that the sample represents the intended population. A large convenience sample can estimate its own biased selection process very precisely while missing the target. Increasing sample size mainly reduces sampling variability under a valid design; it does not automatically repair nonresponse, measurement error or systematic exclusion. Report the estimate, uncertainty method, units and important assumptions together. Distinguish practical importance from statistical detectability, and avoid turning a failure to detect a difference into proof of exact equality. A useful analysis explains what additional data or design improvement would address the most important remaining limitation.

notes.heading: Reducing sampling variation without repairing bias
paragraphs: Under an independent identically distributed sampling model, the standard error of a mean scales as the population standard deviation divided by the square root of sample size. Replacing the unknown population spread with a sample estimate adds an estimation step. Increasing sample size can reduce random sampling variation while leaving systematic selection or measurement bias intact. A large volunteer survey may give a precise estimate for its respondents without representing nonrespondents. State the sampling model before interpreting a narrow interval, and keep confidence in a procedure distinct from a probability that a fixed parameter moves between intervals. The arithmetic here isolates the standard-error scaling rather than certifying a real survey.

workedExamples.prompt: For independent observations with population standard deviation 12 and sample size 36, calculate the standard error of the mean.
steps: Use σ/√n under the stated assumptions.
workedExamples.answer: 2 in the same units as the observations.

workedExamples.prompt: Under the same independent-sampling model, what sample-size multiplier halves the standard error?
steps: Doubling √n requires multiplying n by four.

workedExamples.prompt: A very large online volunteer survey gives a narrow interval for an attitude estimate. Explain one reason it may still poorly represent all residents.
steps: Participation is self-selected rather than necessarily representative.
People with internet access or strong opinions may be included at different rates.
A narrow sampling interval does not by itself correct that selection bias.
workedExamples.answer: Precision conditional on the sample does not establish representativeness of the target population.

workedExamples.prompt: Under an independent sampling model with population standard deviation 12 units, compare the standard error of the mean for n = 36 and n = 144.
workedExamples.answer: The standard errors are 2 units and 1 unit respectively.
steps: Quadrupling sample size halves the standard error under this model.

misconceptions.claim: The standard error is the spread of individual observations in one sample.
misconceptions.correction: It describes the sampling variation of a statistic; individual spread is a different quantity.

misconceptions.claim: A larger sample automatically removes selection bias.
misconceptions.correction: A biased sampling mechanism can remain biased at very large sample sizes.

flashcards.front: How does a parameter differ from a statistic?
flashcards.back: A parameter describes the target population or model; a statistic is calculated from a sample.

flashcards.front: What varies in a sampling distribution of the mean?
flashcards.back: The sample mean across repetitions of the specified sampling procedure.

flashcards.front: Under independent common-variance sampling, what is the standard error of the mean?
flashcards.back: σ/√n, where σ is the population standard deviation.

flashcards.front: What sample-size change halves standard error under that model?
What does 95% coverage describe in a frequentist confidence procedure?
flashcards.back: The long-run proportion of constructed intervals containing the fixed parameter under the procedure's assumptions.

flashcards.front: Why can a very narrow interval still be misleading?
flashcards.back: It may omit systematic sampling or measurement bias and rely on assumptions that do not hold.

flashcards.front: How much must sample size increase to halve standard error under the same independent model?
flashcards.back: By a factor of four, with the population spread held fixed.

flashcards.front: Can a narrow sampling interval coexist with substantial bias?
flashcards.back: Yes. An interval calculation can omit systematic selection or measurement error.

questions.prompt: Which distribution describes the values of a sample mean across repeated samples?
options: Only the observed histogram of individual values
The sampling distribution of the mean
questions.answer: The sampling distribution of the mean
solution: Each repeated sample produces a statistic.
The distribution of those statistics is its sampling distribution.
markingPoints: Select the sampling distribution of the mean.

questions.prompt: For 64 independent observations with common population standard deviation 16, calculate the standard error of the mean.
solution: Use 16/√64 under the stated independent-sampling assumptions.

questions.prompt: Explain why doubling sample size does not halve the standard error of the mean under the independent common-variance model.
questions.answer: Standard error scales with 1/√n, so doubling n multiplies it by 1/√2, not 1/2. Halving it requires four times n.
solution: Compare the effect of doubling with the required fourfold increase.
markingPoints: Identify the required multiplier for halving.

questions.prompt: Interpret a 95% confidence procedure without claiming that a fixed parameter has a 95% frequentist probability of lying inside one observed interval.
questions.answer: Under the procedure's assumptions, approximately 95% of intervals formed over repeated samples contain the fixed parameter. The realised interval either contains it or does not; the percentage describes the method's long-run coverage.
solution: Describe repetition of the sampling and interval procedure.
Keep the target parameter fixed in that interpretation.
State the long-run coverage claim and its assumptions.
markingPoints: Distinguish fixed parameter from varying intervals.

questions.prompt: A researcher replaces a small representative sample with a huge convenience sample and claims accuracy must improve. Evaluate the claim.
questions.answer: The larger sample may reduce random variability within its selection process, but convenience selection can introduce systematic bias relative to the target population. Accuracy depends on the design and measurement as well as sample size, so the claim is not guaranteed.
solution: Recognise the possible reduction in variability.
Identify the unresolved or increased selection bias.
Evaluate accuracy using both rather than sample size alone.

questions.prompt: Under an independent sampling model with population standard deviation 12 units, compare the standard error of the mean for n = 36 and n = 144.
questions.answer: The standard errors are 2 units and 1 unit respectively.
solution: Quadrupling sample size halves the standard error under this model.
markingPoints: Quadrupling sample size halves the standard error under this model.

questions.prompt: A voluntary online survey quadruples its response count and claims selection bias has therefore halved. Explain why the standard-error calculation does not justify that claim.
questions.answer: The square-root rule concerns random sampling variation under a model, not systematic differences between volunteers and the target population.
solution: Volunteer recruitment can select people with different responses from nonparticipants.
More responses do not necessarily change that selection mechanism.
Assess representativeness separately from any model-based standard-error reduction.
markingPoints: Volunteer recruitment can select people with different responses from nonparticipants.
More responses do not necessarily change that selection mechanism.
Assess representativeness separately from any model-based standard-error reduction.

revisionChecklist: Name the population, sampling design and statistic.
State assumptions before using a standard-error formula.
Separate precision, bias, practical importance and coverage interpretation.
Explain the reasoning in “Separate precision and representativeness” and correct the linked error-analysis response without copying its solution.
